indexing.note: scheduled (Act 46, SLH 2024): new tables for 2025-2026, 2027-2028 and from 2029; the first band ends at 9,600 / 14,400 / 19,200 single and separate, 19,200 / 28,800 / 38,400 joint; rates unchanged (HRS 235-51)
fixed by statute: one more exemption of 1,144 (HRS 235-54(a))

not_modelled.what: Alternative tax on capital gains (Tax on Capital Gains Worksheet): when taxable income is over 24,000 single or married filing separately, 36,000 head of household, 48,000 joint, the net long-term gain above the greater of the ordinary income or that amount may be taxed at 7.25%, and the tax is the smaller of that computation and the schedule tax. The projection's capital_gains field holds a fixed extra rate, deducted share or exemption, not a smaller-of cap, so gains run through the brackets.

The exclusion ratio of HAR 18-235-7-03 (Department of Taxation amendment effective 1/1/98): a private plan distribution is excluded only in the ratio of employer contributions to employer plus pretax employee plus previously taxed contributions. 401(k), 457 and SEP salary-reduction deferrals are pretax employee contributions and taxable; employer matching and profit-sharing money is excluded. A projection does not know a plan's employer-funded share, so employer_plan_distribution (401(k), 403(b), 457, Thrift Savings Plan) is taxed in full, which overstates tax by the employer-funded share; and a private pension is excluded in full even when the employee contributed (pension_contributory is asked only for public plans), which understates tax by the employee-funded share.

The exclusion ratio of HAR 18-235-7-03 (Department of Taxation amendment effective 1/1/98): a private plan distribution is excluded only in the ratio of employer contributions to employer plus pretax employee plus previously taxed contributions. 401(k), 457 and SEP salary-reduction deferrals are pretax employee contributions and taxable; employer matching and profit-sharing money is excluded. A projection does not know a plan's employer-funded share, so employer_plan_distribution (401(k), 403(b), 457, Thrift Savings Plan) is taxed in full, which overstates tax by the employer-funded share; and a private pension is excluded in full even when the employee contributed (pension_contributory is asked only for public plans), which understates tax by the employee-funded share.

A rollover IRA keeps the character of the money rolled in (booklet line 13, Nontaxable Rollover IRAs; HAR 18-235-7-03): money from a qualifying employer-funded plan stays exempt, also when converted to a Roth IRA; money from 401(k), 457 or SEP salary-reduction deferrals, and IRAs the employer did not fund, are pretax employee contributions and taxable. A projection does not know where IRA money came from, so every IRA distribution and Roth conversion is taxed, which overstates tax by the employer-funded money in it.
Dependent exemption of 1,144 per child or other dependent (line 6c, 6d).
Disability exemption of 7,000 per blind, deaf or totally disabled person certified on Form N-172, in lieu of the 1,144 exemption and the age-65 exemption.
First 8,636 of military reserve or Hawaii national guard duty pay per member is excluded (line 15).
Interest on U.S. obligations (Treasury bills and notes, U.S. Savings Bonds) is subtracted (line 18).

approximations.what: The alternative tax on capital gains is not applied (not_modelled): long-term gains are taxed by the schedules.
approximations.size: Up to 3.75 points (11% top rate against 7.25%) on gains in the top band. A single filer with 400,000 of taxable income including 100,000 of long-term gain: schedule tax 34,216, worksheet tax 30,716, overstated by 3,500. Small or nothing where the gain sits in the 7.6% band or below.

approximations.what: Employer-plan distributions (employer_plan_distribution: 401(k), 403(b), 457, Thrift Savings Plan) are taxed in full. HAR 18-235-7-03 excludes their employer-funded share, in the exclusion ratio of employer contributions to employer plus pretax employee plus previously taxed contributions; the projection does not know that share. The employee's own deferrals are pretax employee contributions and are rightly taxed.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the employer-funded share, e.g. employer matching or profit-sharing money; nothing for a plan funded only by the employee's deferrals. Example: a single retiree whose 401(k) was funded by a 6% deferral and a 3% employer match (exclusion ratio 3/9, one third) withdraws 30,000 on top of 60,000 of other taxable income: 10,000 is excludable and is taxed at 7.6%, overstating tax by 760 a year (1,100 in the 11% band). The Department of Taxation's 2026-07-14 Tax Review Commission presentation calls 401(k) withdrawals fully taxable, so in practice the overstatement may be less.

approximations.what: IRA distributions and Roth conversions are taxed in full, including money rolled over from a qualifying employer-funded plan, which keeps its exclusion (booklet line 13, Nontaxable Rollover IRAs; HAR 18-235-7-03). IRAs the employer did not fund and rolled-over 401(k), 457 or SEP deferrals are pretax employee contributions and are rightly taxed.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the employer-funded money withdrawn or converted. Example (the booklet's): a 50,000 Roth conversion of an IRA holding a lump sum from an employer-funded profit-sharing plan paid upon retirement is fully exempt; for a joint couple with 100,000 of other taxable income it is taxed at 7.6%, overstating tax by 3,800. A rollover of a 401(k) with a one-third employer match overstates by a third of that, about 1,267. Nothing for an IRA funded by the owner's own contributions.

approximations.what: A private pension is excluded in full. HAR 18-235-7-03 excludes a contributory private pension only in its exclusion ratio (the booklet: 'partially taxed by Hawaii if the employee contributed', Schedule J); the projection cannot tell a contributory private plan (pension_contributory is asked only for public plans), so it treats every private pension as wholly employer-funded. A private defined benefit pension wholly funded by the employer is excluded in full, as the rule says.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the employee-funded share. Example: a 30,000 private defined benefit pension in which the employee made 20% of the contributions (exclusion ratio 0.8): about 6,000 is taxable; for a single filer with 50,000 of other taxable income it falls in the 7.6% band, understating tax by about 456 a year. Nothing for a plan the employee did not contribute to.

approximations.what: Government and private pensions are exempt whatever the age; early distributions subject to the 10% federal penalty tax, and government plan distributions from voluntary employee contributions under an elective right, are taxable and are not separated.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on such distributions; rare for a retiree drawing a pension upon retirement.

approximations.what: Railroad retirement is exempt in full; the booklet names only first tier Railroad Retirement Act benefits, and Tier 2 is not stated.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on Tier 2 benefits, if Hawaii taxes them.

approximations.what: The standard deduction is always taken; Hawaii itemized deductions (and their limit above 166,800 of Hawaii AGI) are not modelled.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the amount by which itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction, for an itemizer.

approximations.what: The standard deduction is applied to a married person filing separately whose spouse itemizes, who must itemize.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the difference between 4,400 and that person's itemized deductions.

approximations.what: Dependent exemptions are not applied (dependents not modelled).
approximations.size: Up to 11% of 1,144 per dependent, about 126 a year.

approximations.what: Interest on U.S. Treasury obligations and savings bonds is taxed (the projection cannot tell it from other interest).
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on the Treasury interest.

approximations.what: Military reserve and Hawaii national guard duty pay is taxed (the exclusion is not modelled).
approximations.size: Up to 11% of 8,636 per member, about 950 a year.

approximations.what: A projection that cannot tell Hawaii bonds from other states' bonds treats all tax-exempt interest as other-state and adds it back.
approximations.size: The Hawaii rate on interest from Hawaii (and Puerto Rico, U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa) obligations.

approximations.what: The age-65 exemption uses the projection's age test (65 or older in the year); the booklet's test is age 65 or over as of January 1 of the following year.
approximations.size: At most one 1,144 exemption in the year a person turns 65, about 126.

approximations.what: Later years (Act 24, 2026): from tax year 2027 a new 13% rate applies above 500,000 single, 750,000 head of household and 1,000,000 joint, and some lower-bracket rates change for 2027-2028 and 2029 on. The projection carries the 2025 schedule (top rate 11%).
approximations.size: Above the new thresholds, 2 points more tax (2,000 per 100,000 of income above 500,000 single); the lower-bracket changes move tax either way by smaller amounts.
